guide.summary: Big Idea 3 is the largest part of the exam (30–35%). It covers variables and assignment, data abstraction with lists, expressions and the MOD operator, Boolean logic, selection, iteration, list traversal, developing and comparing algorithms, binary search, procedures with parameters and return values, libraries, random values and simulations, algorithmic efficiency, heuristics, and undecidable problems.

sections.heading: Variables, expressions, and lists
sections.body: a ← expression evaluates the right side and stores it in a; a variable holds only its most recent value, and assigning b ← a copies the value at that moment. Arithmetic includes MOD (remainder): 17 MOD 5 is 2. Lists are ordered and 1-indexed in AP pseudocode: list[1] is the first element; accessing an index less than 1 or greater than LENGTH(list) causes an error. INSERT(list, i, value) shifts later elements right; APPEND adds to the end; REMOVE(list, i) shifts later elements left. Lists are a data abstraction: one name manages many values, so code doesn't depend on how many items there are.

sections.heading: Selection and iteration
sections.body: IF/ELSE chooses between paths based on a Boolean expression; nested conditionals handle multiple cases. Boolean operators: NOT, AND, OR. REPEAT n TIMES runs a fixed number of times; REPEAT UNTIL(condition) checks the condition before each iteration and stops when it becomes true (it may run zero times or forever). FOR EACH item IN list visits every element. Common algorithms: sum, average, max/min, count, filter, and check whether a condition holds for any or all elements. When removing elements during traversal, only advance the index if nothing was removed.

sections.heading: Procedures, libraries, and simulations
sections.body: Procedures (functions) are named groups of instructions that can take parameters and RETURN values; they provide procedural abstraction, letting programmers use a procedure knowing what it does, not how, and change its implementation without affecting callers. Parameters generalize a procedure for different inputs. Libraries and APIs provide prewritten procedures. RANDOM(a, b) returns a random integer from a to b inclusive; simulations use random values to model real-world events, trading accuracy for simplicity, and may be repeated many times.

sections.heading: Searching and efficiency
sections.body: Linear search checks elements in order and works on unsorted lists. Binary search requires a sorted list and halves the search range each step: at most about log₂ n + 1 checks, far fewer than linear search for large lists. Algorithms that run in polynomial time are reasonable; exponential or factorial time is unreasonable for large inputs. Heuristics find approximate solutions when exact ones take too long (e.g., route planning). Some problems are undecidable: no algorithm can solve every instance (e.g., determining whether any program halts).

keyTakeaways: REPEAT UNTIL checks before each pass.
Reasonable = polynomial; heuristics for hard problems; some problems are undecidable.
commonMistakes: Thinking REPEAT UNTIL runs while the condition is true.
Assuming b changes when a is reassigned after b ← a.
Applying binary search to unsorted data.
examTips: Trace with a table of variables and list contents after each line.
For 'which code segment works' questions, test with a small example including edge cases.
Simulations: check that random ranges match the intended probabilities.
Count binary-search steps by repeated halving.
guide.cramSheet:
**Assign:** a ← expr · copies value · MOD remainder

**Lists:** 1-indexed · INSERT shifts right · REMOVE shifts left · APPEND end · LENGTH

**Control:** IF/ELSE · REPEAT n TIMES · REPEAT UNTIL (stop when true) · FOR EACH

**Procedures:** parameters · RETURN · abstraction · libraries/APIs

**Random:** RANDOM(a, b) inclusive · simulations

**Search:** linear (any) · binary (sorted, log₂ n)

**Efficiency:** polynomial reasonable · exponential unreasonable · heuristics · undecidable

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Describe the purpose of the penalty parameter and how a call with penalty 0 differs from a call with penalty 5.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain the role of the selection statement in the procedure.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: If answers = ["A", "C", "B"] and responses = ["A", "B", "B"], what does score(answers, responses, 5) return? Show how you determined it.

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: Identify a condition that would cause an error, and describe how to modify the code to prevent it.

rubric.description: penalty is the number of points subtracted for each wrong answer; penalty 0 never subtracts, while penalty 5 lowers the score by 5 for every miss.
The IF compares each response to the correct answer to decide whether to add 10 points or subtract the penalty.
If responses is shorter than answers, responses[i] is out of range. Fix: before comparing, check IF (i ≤ LENGTH(responses)) and only then compare responses[i] (treat missing responses as wrong).

practice.sampleResponse:
a. penalty controls how many points are taken away for each incorrect answer. With score(answers, responses, 0), wrong answers simply earn nothing; with penalty 5, each wrong answer reduces the total by 5, so the same responses earn a lower score.

b. The IF/ELSE compares the player's response to the correct answer at the same position. If they match, 10 points are added; otherwise the penalty is subtracted. This determines how each question affects the total.

c. Question 1: "A" = "A", +10 (points = 10). Question 2: "B" ≠ "C", −5 (points = 5). Question 3: "B" = "B", +10 (points = 15). The procedure returns 15.

d. If the player skips the last question so responses has fewer elements than answers, responses[i] will be accessed with an index larger than LENGTH(responses), causing an error. I could wrap the comparison in an outer IF (i ≤ LENGTH(responses)) and subtract the penalty in its ELSE branch, so missing responses count as incorrect without accessing an invalid index.
